summary: Harrer and Wider argue data contracts apply API-design practice to datasets and become essential when consumers are agents: a human who distrusts data hesitates or asks the owner, while an agent 'treats every value as truth' and produces confidently wrong results. ODCS (Bitol project, Linux Foundation) is now the de facto standard after ODCS 3.1 support in Data Contract CLI retired the older Data Contract Specification; ODCS 3.2 (2026) added an AI context section. Example contract fields: schema/quality, owner and support channels, terms of use and SLAs, server locations (test/staging/prod as separate server entries), roles mapping to platform IAM roles (e.g. Snowflake), AI context, price (e.g. 10 USD per TB scanned), custom properties. Practices: contract-first vs data-first; keep contracts in the pipeline repo; SemVer with breaking changes shipped as a new major version alongside a new dataset and phased in/out (draft->active->deprecated->retired); for event streams use forward/full compatibility (warning: schema-registry backward-compat default permits field deletion, which breaks consumers); exclude SELECT * so adding columns is non-breaking. Access agreements: bilateral, provider-approved, time-bound (for agents possibly a few minutes); Open Access Agreement Standard is an RFC. Costs acknowledged: not worth writing for every dataset.

pub_date: 2026-11-18 (confirmed via page datePublished; date-only, so may predate the ~09:00 UTC Edition 2 send, but URL not in Edition 2)
what_changed: First application of Epoch's Inference Performance Index (IPI, introduced Nov 9) to its AI Chip Sales dataset: installed agentic-inference capacity grew 4.6× (Q2 2025 -> Q2 2026) vs 2.6× for peak 8-bit FLOP/s, i.e. FLOP/s understates growth in serving capacity for long-context, cached agent workloads.
mechanism: Per-chip IPI scores (v1, in GB300-equivalents) measured on a fixed basket of agentic workloads with long cached contexts, accounting for memory, inter-chip communication and lower precision, both prefill and decode; multiplied by cumulative chips sold per family and summed. Growth is driven mostly by the Hopper-to-Blackwell transition: GB300 ~8× the inference capacity of H200 per GPU vs only ~2.2× from GB300 to Vera Rubin VR200 (modeled).
evidence_quality: Modeled estimate with stated assumptions and uncertainty intervals (90% UI 4.2-5.1× inference, 2.5-2.7× peak compute). Key judgment assumptions: 60/40 GB-NVL72 vs B/HGX split, even H100/H200 split from Q4 2024. Software efficiency not modeled; UI excludes uncertainty in modeled per-chip performance.
independent_confirmation: None independent; builds on Epoch's own IPI report (Nov 9) and AI Chip Sales dataset.
relevance: Medium: useful context for inference economics and why prefix/KV caching and memory bandwidth matter more than FLOP/s for agent serving; ties to Edition 2's prefix-caching and inference-economics thread. Not directly actionable.
overlap_with_prior: Related to Edition 2 prefix caching / Pragmatic Engineer inference deepdive; URL not previously used.
summary: Between Q2 2025 and Q2 2026 the estimated agentic inference capacity of all AI chips sold to date grew 4.6× while peak 8-bit compute grew 2.6× (total ~6.67M GB300e in Q2 2026 vs ~1.45M in Q2 2025; peak compute ~3.2e7 vs 1.2e7 H100e). Blackwell + Blackwell Ultra account for 74% of added capacity and ~73% of total agentic inference capacity by Q2 2026 vs 50% of peak compute. GB300 delivers ~8× H200 inference capacity per GPU. Inference capacity per unit of peak compute rose ~77% over the year ('hardware-model co-design': bigger scale-up domains, lower precision, architectures that use hardware better). Chips sold in Q2 2026 added 3.3× the capacity of those sold in Q2 2025, below the 4.6× total, so Epoch expects growth to slow; regression of log additions gives 3.2×/yr for inference capacity and 2.1×/yr for peak compute (Q1 2024-Q2 2026 window: 6.8× and 2.5×/yr, doubling times 4.3 and 9.2 months). Sustaining 4.6× would need annual additions of 3.6× the starting base. Modeled gain GB300 -> VR200 is only 2.2× per GPU. Sensitivity: 90% UI 4.2-5.1× (inference) and 2.5-2.7× (peak); earlier H200 transition scenario gives 4.5×. Limitations: judgment-based rack/server split, H100/H200 split, no software efficiency modelling.

title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
author: Airbnb engineers with AWS (AWS ML blog)
what_changed: Airbnb publishes its operating method for internal coding agents (AirChat): eval-measured cost per task drives model defaults and gateway-enforced reasoning-effort ceilings, then production CloudWatch/gateway telemetry is compared against eval expectations.
mechanism: Cost per task = list-price cost of all four token classes (uncached input, cache read, cache write, output) summed over every request in a task. Seven eval suites in Harbor format (instruction.md, task.toml, Dockerfile, grader, reference solution); 8-dimension weighted model-graded rubric with a ceiling (autonomy 0/0.5 caps score at 25/100). Derived OTPS = OutputTokenCount/(InvocationLatency-TimeToFirstToken)*1000. Explains Bedrock TPM quota reservation (uncached input + cache writes + max_tokens reserved up front; cache reads never count; output burndown multipliers).
evidence_quality: Practitioner-measured production data from a named customer, published on vendor (AWS) blog; figures are relative (no absolute dollars).
relevance: Very high: concrete, reusable recipe for coding-agent cost governance, eval-to-production comparison, latency triage and throttling diagnosis.
overlap_with_prior: Thematic overlap with Ed2 TokenEconomizer and Databricks AI Index (coding-agent tokenomics) but different, operational angle; new.
summary: Thousands of Airbnb engineers use AirChat weekly; all requests route through an LLM gateway on Bedrock. Eight new models shipped in ~5 weeks; by mid-October ~2/3 of coding-agent requests went to those new models. On one model, low->high reasoning effort raised score by 0.8 points but cost per task 2.5x, so effort ceilings are gateway-enforced. New-model eval campaigns produce first results within hours and full suite scores + cost per task by next morning. Key cautionary tale: 'model A' scored >3 points above the prior best at about the same eval cost per task, but in production weekly spend per user was several times higher: each request cost ~3x and users sent ~3x as many requests, because long self-directed sessions re-read cached context (output tokens were only ~1/10 of request cost). A newer model scoring higher at ~1/6 the cost per task replaced it via config change; the heavy-user group's spend on their main model fell to ~1/7 in the first full week with similar request counts. Latency case: latency +40% with flat TTFT and OTPS was traced to a system-prompt change that raised output tokens per request 50% - treat prompt changes and model upgrades as deploys. Prereqs: invocation logging (off by default; holds full prompts), tagged IAM roles with cost-allocation tags activated before collection (no backfill), dated list-price table.
